lessons.title: Common Timber Pests in Africa: Termites, Borers, and Fungi
lessons.body: In Africa, timber structures face three main enemies: termites, borers, and fungi. Termites are the most destructive. Subterranean termites build mud tubes from soil to wood, eating from the inside out. Drywood termites leave small holes and frass (sawdust-like pellets). In West and Central Africa, Macrotermes species can destroy a door frame in months. Borers are beetle larvae that tunnel into wood, leaving 2-3mm holes and fine dust. The African powder-post beetle attacks dry seasoned wood, while the longhorn beetle prefers moist timber. Fungi cause rot, appearing as white or brown patches. Brown rot makes wood crumbly; white rot makes it spongy. Fungi need moisture above 20% and temperatures between 20-30Â°Câcommon in humid regions. To identify pests: look for mud tubes (termites), exit holes (borers), or soft, discolored wood (fungi). Tap timber with a hammerâa dull thud means internal damage. Probe with a screwdriver; if it sinks easily, rot or termites are present. Prevention starts with keeping timber dry. Use treated wood, elevate posts off the ground, and ensure ventilation. In storage, stack timber with spacers to allow airflow. For active infestations, remove and burn damaged wood. For termites, apply termiticide like imidacloprid or fipronil to the soil and wood. For borers, inject insecticide into holes or fumigate. For fungi, cut out rot and treat with fungicide. Always wear gloves and a mask when handling chemicals. Local solutions include neem oil, which repels termites, and cashew nut shell liquid, a natural preservative. Remember: pests are easier to prevent than to eliminate. Inspect your timber at least twice a year, especially after the rainy season.

lessons.title: Applying Natural and Chemical Preservatives
lessons.body: Preservatives protect timber from pests and rot. You can use natural or chemical methods. Natural preservatives are cheap and locally available. Neem oil: crush neem seeds, soak in water for 24 hours, strain, and brush onto wood. It repels termites and borers. Cashew nut shell liquid (CNSL): a dark oil from cashew processing, mix with diesel (1:1) and paint on timber. It waterproofs and kills insects. Tannins from acacia bark: boil bark in water, reduce, and apply as a stain. For chemical preservatives, three types are common: water-based (e.g., copper chrome arsenate, CCA), oil-based (creosote, pentachlorophenol), and solvent-based (permethrin). CCA is effective but toxicâhandle with gloves and mask. Creosote smells strong but protects against moisture and insects; use only outdoors. Permethrin is safer for indoor use. Application methods: brushing is simplest for small areas; dip for 5-10 minutes for posts; pressure treatment forces preservative deep into woodâbest for structural timber. For a door frame, brush two coats of preservative, allowing 24 hours drying between coats. Mix your own borate solution: 1 kg borax, 1 kg boric acid, 10 liters water. Soak timber for 24 hours. This is low-toxicity and effective against fungi and borers. Always treat cut ends and jointsâthey absorb water. After treatment, let timber dry completely before painting or installing. Safety: wear gloves, goggles, and a dust mask. Do not eat or smoke while handling chemicals. Store preservatives away from children and animals. In Africa, many artisans use spent engine oil as a preservativeâit works but is toxic and pollutes soil. Avoid it. Instead, use neem or borate for family homes. For heavy structural timber, invest in CCA or creosote. Reapply preservative every 3-5 years, especially in coastal or humid areas. Test effectiveness by checking for new pest holes after 6 months.

lessons.title: Repairing Rotting or Broken Timber Beams
lessons.body: When a timber beam rots or breaks, you can repair it instead of replacing the whole piece. First, assess the damage. Probe with an awl or screwdriver. If rot is soft and spongy, it must be removed. For minor rot (less than 20% of cross-section), cut out the rotten wood with a chisel and mallet. Use a wire brush to clean the area. Treat with fungicide and let dry. Then fill with epoxy wood filler or a mixture of sawdust and wood glue. For structural beams, you need a stronger repair. If a beam is broken or has major rot, use a 'sister' beam: cut a new piece of timber the same size, treat it, and bolt it alongside the damaged section with 12mm galvanized bolts every 300mm. Use washers under bolt heads. For a split beam, wrap it with a metal plate and bolt through. Another method is 'scarf joint': cut matching angled ends on both pieces, apply waterproof glue, and bolt together. For a post that has rotted at the base, cut off the bottom 300mm, treat the cut, and set the post on a concrete plinth or metal shoe. Never bury untreated timber in soil. If the beam is load-bearing, support the structure with temporary props before starting. Use acrow props or wooden posts. Work from the top down. After repair, apply preservative to all new cuts. Check the repair monthly for the first year. In rural areas, you can use local hardwoods like mvule or iroko for repairsâthey are naturally durable. Avoid softwoods like pine unless treated. For a quick fix, wrap the beam with bitumen felt and wireâbut this is temporary. Proper repair saves money and preserves the building's character. Always wear gloves and eye protection when cutting or drilling. If unsure, consult a carpenter or engineer.

lessons.title: Jointing Techniques for Structural Timber
lessons.body: Strong joints are critical for structural timber. Weak joints cause sagging and collapse. Here are five practical joints for African conditions. 1) Mortise and tenon: cut a rectangular hole (mortise) in one timber and a matching projection (tenon) on the other. Glue and pin with a wooden peg or bolt. Use for beams and posts. 2) Lap joint: cut half the thickness from each timber where they overlap, then bolt or screw together. Good for splicing beams. 3) Scarf joint: for joining two beams end-to-end. Cut angled steps (1:6 slope) on each end, glue, and bolt. This resists tension. 4) Dovetail joint: interlocking wedge shapes, used for corner joints in frames. Strong against pulling apart. 5) Bolted joint: simplestâoverlap timbers and drill 12-16mm holes, insert galvanized bolts with washers, and tighten. Use at least two bolts per joint. For all joints, apply waterproof wood glue (e.g., polyurethane) before assembling. Clamp until dry (24 hours). Pre-drill holes to avoid splitting. Use galvanized or stainless steel fixingsâplain steel rusts in humidity. In termite-prone areas, wrap joints with bitumen tape or apply preservative after assembly. For heavy loads, add metal plates (gang nails or T-straps) on both sides. Check joints annually for looseness. Tighten bolts and replace rusty ones. In traditional African construction, joints are often lashed with rope or rawhideâthese work for light loads but not for structural beams. For modern buildings, use mechanical fasteners. Always ensure joints are not in contact with soil or concrete. If timber is green (unseasoned), allow for shrinkageâuse washers and re-tighten after 6 months. Practice on scrap wood before working on a building. A good joint is tight, flush, and treated.

lessons.title: Protecting Timber from Moisture and Sun
lessons.body: Moisture and sun are timber's silent enemies. Moisture causes rot, fungi, and termites. Sun causes cracking, warping, and fading. To protect timber, control water and shade. First, design to shed water. Use roof overhangs of at least 600mm. Slope surfaces so water runs off. For posts, set them on concrete plinths or metal basesânever directly in soil. If in soil, use a concrete collar and treat the post with creosote. For beams, ensure no water traps. Drill weep holes in horizontal timbers. Second, apply finishes. Paint or varnish creates a barrier. Use exterior-grade paint with fungicide. For natural look, apply linseed oil or tung oil every year. For decks, use a water-repellent sealer. Third, ventilate. In roofs, leave a 50mm gap between insulation and roofing. In walls, use breathable membranes. Fourth, control ground moisture. Install drainage around foundations. Use gutters and downpipes to direct water away. Fifth, protect from sun. In hot climates, use light-colored paint to reflect heat. Plant trees for shade but keep branches 2m from timber to allow airflow. For timber in direct sun, apply UV-resistant varnish. Sixth, inspect after rains. Look for damp patches, mold, or soft wood. Dry wet timber within 24 hours. Use a fan or sunlight. Seventh, use naturally durable species: teak, iroko, mahogany, or mvule. These resist moisture and insects. For less durable woods, treat with preservative. In coastal areas, salt air accelerates corrosionâuse stainless steel fixings. In desert areas, sun is the main threatâuse thick sections and shade. In rainforests, moisture is constantâuse elevated structures and good drainage. Remember: water is the enemy. Keep timber dry and it will last decades.

lessons.title: Workshop: Treating a Timber Door Frame
lessons.body: In this workshop, you will treat a timber door frame. You need: a door frame (or a 2m x 1m frame), sandpaper (80 and 120 grit), brush, gloves, mask, preservative (borate solution or commercial wood preservative), wood filler, caulk, and paint. Step 1: Inspect. Check for rot, termite damage, or cracks. Probe with a screwdriver. If soft, cut out and replace that section. Step 2: Clean. Remove old paint with a scraper or sandpaper. Sand the frame smooth. Wipe with a damp cloth. Step 3: Treat. Mix borate solution: 1 kg borax, 1 kg boric acid, 10 liters water. Apply liberally with a brush, especially on cut ends and joints. Let dry for 24 hours. For chemical preservative, follow label instructions. Step 4: Repair. Fill cracks and holes with epoxy wood filler. Let dry, then sand smooth. Step 5: Seal. Apply a coat of primer, then two coats of exterior paint. Pay attention to the bottom of the frameâwater collects there. Step 6: Install. If installing, ensure the frame is plumb and level. Use galvanized screws. Seal gaps with caulk. Step 7: Maintain. Check every 6 months. Reapply preservative every 2-3 years. For a door frame in a humid area, use a raised threshold and a drip cap above the door. If termites are a problem, apply a termiticide barrier around the base. Safety: wear gloves, mask, and goggles. Work in a ventilated area. Do not eat or smoke. Clean up spills. Dispose of waste properly. This workshop takes about 4 hours plus drying time. By treating your door frame, you extend its life by 10-15 years. Practice on a small piece first. Take photos before and after to show your work.

quiz.q: Which pest builds mud tubes from soil to wood?
quiz.explanation: Subterranean termites construct mud tubes to travel from soil to timber.

quiz.q: What is a sign of drywood termites?
quiz.explanation: Drywood termites leave small holes and frass (sawdust-like pellets).

quiz.q: Which fungus makes wood crumbly and brown?
quiz.explanation: Brown rot causes wood to become crumbly and brown.

quiz.q: What moisture level supports fungal growth?
quiz.explanation: Fungi need moisture above 20% to thrive.

quiz.q: Which tool helps detect internal damage in timber?
quiz.explanation: A screwdriver can probe for softness or hollow areas.

quiz.q: Which natural preservative repels termites?
quiz.explanation: Neem oil is a natural termite repellent.

quiz.q: What is the ratio for a borate solution?
options: A) 1 kg borax, 1 kg boric acid, 10 L water
B) 2 kg borax, 1 kg boric acid, 5 L water
C) 1 kg borax, 2 kg boric acid, 10 L water
D) 0.5 kg borax, 0.5 kg boric acid, 5 L water
quiz.explanation: The standard borate mix is 1:1:10 (borax:boric acid:water).

quiz.q: Which preservative is safest for indoor use?
quiz.explanation: Permethrin is a solvent-based preservative safe for indoor use.

quiz.q: How long should you soak timber in borate solution?
quiz.explanation: Soaking for 24 hours allows deep penetration.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling chemical preservatives?
quiz.explanation: Gloves, goggles, and a mask protect against toxic chemicals.

quiz.q: What is the first step in repairing a rotting beam?
quiz.explanation: Assessing damage determines the repair method.

quiz.q: What is a 'sister' beam?
options: A) A beam that is split
B) A new beam bolted alongside a damaged one
C) A beam made of two pieces
quiz.explanation: A sister beam is a new timber bolted to the damaged section for support.

quiz.q: What is a scarf joint used for?
quiz.explanation: A scarf joint joins two beams end-to-end.

quiz.q: What is the minimum bolt size for structural timber joints?
quiz.explanation: 12mm galvanized bolts are recommended for structural joints.

quiz.q: Which joint is strongest against pulling apart?
quiz.explanation: Dovetail joints interlock and resist tension.

quiz.q: What should you apply to joints before assembly?
quiz.explanation: Waterproof wood glue strengthens the joint.

quiz.q: Why use galvanized fixings?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized fixings resist corrosion in humid conditions.

quiz.q: What is the minimum roof overhang to protect timber?
quiz.explanation: A 600mm overhang helps shed water away from timber.

quiz.q: How should posts be set to avoid moisture?
quiz.explanation: Concrete plinths keep timber off the ground and dry.

quiz.q: Which finish protects timber from UV?
quiz.explanation: UV-resistant varnish protects against sun damage.

quiz.q: What should you do after rains?
quiz.explanation: Inspect after rains to catch moisture problems early.

quiz.q: Which wood is naturally durable?
quiz.explanation: Iroko is naturally resistant to rot and insects.

quiz.q: What is the first step in treating a door frame?
quiz.explanation: Inspection identifies damage before treatment.

quiz.q: What mix is used for borate treatment in the workshop?
options: A) 1 kg borax, 1 kg boric acid, 10 L water
B) 2 kg borax, 1 kg boric acid, 5 L water
C) 1 kg borax, 2 kg boric acid, 10 L water
D) 0.5 kg borax, 0.5 kg boric acid, 5 L water
quiz.explanation: The workshop uses the standard 1:1:10 borate mix.

quiz.q: How long should preservative dry before painting?
quiz.explanation: Allow 24 hours for preservative to dry before painting.

quiz.q: What should you use to fill cracks in a door frame?
quiz.explanation: Epoxy wood filler is strong and sandable.

quiz.q: How often should you reapply preservative to a door frame?
quiz.explanation: Reapply every 2-3 years for continued protection.

quiz.q: What is a sign of borer infestation?
options: B) Fine dust and small holes
quiz.explanation: Borers leave fine dust and small exit holes.

quiz.q: Which chemical is toxic and should be avoided for family homes?
quiz.explanation: Spent engine oil is toxic and pollutes soil.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a drip cap above a door?
quiz.explanation: A drip cap directs water away from the door frame.
